newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi tells hard left enough is enough.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi tells hard left enough is enough.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi told Italy's parliament on Thursday he would brook no more dissent from his troublesome hard left allies as he battled to re-unite his divided coalition.

Communist Refoundation pushed the government to the brink of collapse earlier this week by refusing to support the deployment of a security force to Albania, but Prodi warned that he would resign if they tried to do the same again.

"Other episodes like that which put this country's international image at risk are unacceptable," Prodi told the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) at the start of a confidence debate in his 11-month old administration.
"We are not here to govern at any cost," he added.
President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro ordered the prime minister to hold confidence votes in both houses of parliament after he had to rely on opposition backing for the Albanian mission.

Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the lower house, backed the government in the first vote in the Senate (upper house) on Thursday and party leader Fausto Bertinotti pledged to do the same when the Chamber votes on Saturday.

But coalition parties were reported to be furious that Prodi had not taken a harder line with Refoundation in a speech to the Senate on Thursday. "It's shameful," Massimo D'Alema, leader of the largest government group, the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), was widely quoted as saying in Friday's newspapers.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, head of the centrist Italian Renewal party, demanded immediate consultations to see if the disparate alliance could carry on.
"The prime minister will not stay in office a minute more if he fails to have a cohesive majority," Dini told reporters.

Prodi agreed that the various government backers should sit down and work out policy, saying the rift with Refoundation was "so serious that we cannot continue without strong, precise and clear clarification" of the terms of the partnership.
Supporters welcomed the speech, which was a tougher version of the one he gave to the Senate on Thursday.
"If the prime minister had used the same political tones in the Senate, many of these problems would have been avoided," said Cesare Salvi, parliamentary party leader of the PDS.
Newspapers thought Prodi would struggle to regain control of the coalition. "The majority in pieces," Corriere della Sera newspaper said in its front page headline.
But the prime minister warned that if his coalition did fall, Italy would lose the chance of becoming a founder member of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"EMU is the primary objective of the government," Prodi said, adding: "Italy needs stability (and) certainty."
However he faces a tough time if he is going to convince the hardline Refoundation to approve plans for a reform of the welfare state. "We cannot wait another day more," Prodi said.
Dini said Refoundation would also have to be more open to a reform of the labour market and stop blocking legislation covering the privatisation of key state companies such as telecoms firm Stet.
"These have been bogged down in parliament because of Refoundation obstructionism," Dini said.
